analysis.one_liner: Bans the President, Congress, senior officials, federal judges, and their families from owning or trading stocks, crypto, and similar investments.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on August 31, 2026 with no cosponsors and referred to four House committees, where it has received no vote or further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal ethics law to bar the President, Vice President, Members of Congress, senior executive branch officials, and federal judges—plus their spouses and dependent children—from owning or trading individual stocks, commodities, futures, digital assets like cryptocurrency, and prediction-market contracts. They would have to sell off those holdings within 30 days, keep only diversified index funds, Treasury and municipal bonds, and small business or personal real estate interests. Officials who fail to divest would owe a daily fine of 10% of the value of their noncompliant holdings, and officials caught trading would forfeit profits plus pay a $10,000 fee. Ethics offices could subpoena brokerage records, and all fines would be published online and deposited for deficit reduction [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens gain a government in which the people setting tax, regulatory, and trade policy cannot personally profit from stock moves, crypto swings, or betting markets those decisions influence; penalties and public fine records also give journalists and voters a check.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary citizens skeptical of officials' conflicts

how_it_helps.text: It bans owning or trading stocks, commodities, futures, digital assets, and event (prediction) contracts by the President, Vice President, Members of Congress, senior executive officials, federal judges, and their spouses and dependents, while allowing diversified index funds, Treasury and municipal bonds, small business interests, and a personal home [S2].

It imposes real teeth: a daily fine equal to 10% of the value of noncompliant holdings (capped at 50%), disgorgement of illegal trading profits plus a $10,000 fee per violation, subpoena power for ethics offices, and public publication of every fine assessed [S2].
It requires divestment within 30 days of enactment or of taking office, and bars officials from paying any penalty with official or campaign funds [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress, senior officials, judges, and their families would bear the cost: they must sell individual stocks and crypto, potentially owing capital-gains taxes on forced sales, and face large daily fines and profit forfeiture if they do not comply.

drawbacks.text: Divestment would be taxed: the bill expressly overrides the existing rule that lets officials defer capital-gains tax on conflict-of-interest sales, so a senior official could owe a large tax bill just to keep their job [S2].

The ban reaches spouses and dependent children, which could force a working spouse to change jobs or liquidate retirement-type investments, and could deter qualified people from serving in senior government roles [S2].
Enforcement depends on supervising ethics offices, whose funding and willingness to use subpoena power would determine whether the penalties are more than paper [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is meaningful: federal officials' financial conflicts of interest are a real and recurring public concern, and an ownership ban with teeth goes further than the current disclosure-and-late-reporting regime. The costs are real but manageable—divesting at fair market value triggers a tax bill the bill makes unavoidable, families holding assets for a working spouse would face disruption, and some capable people might decline senior government jobs rather than sell. The bigger problem is not design but fate: with zero cosponsors and no committee action, its careful drafting may never get an up-or-down vote.

outcome.mechanism: A single House member introduced it, no one signed on, and it went to four committees that have not moved it, so it has not come to a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 31, 2026 and referred the same day to four committees: Oversight and Government Reform, House Administration, Judiciary, and Ways and Means [S4].
As of the latest record, no member has cosponsored the bill [S3].
The action history shows no hearings, no markups, no committee vote, and no floor action since referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and senior officials who want to keep trading individual stocks, since the rules they operate under are unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officials who kept their trading freedoms

for.name: Rep. Eugene Vindman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and submitted it for referral to four House committees [S1][S2].

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no other member has cosponsored, so the partisan shape of support and opposition is not yet visible in the record.

industries.industry: Members of Congress and senior federal officials (as a class)
industries.note: The bill's direct targets: it would force them to sell individual stocks, crypto, and derivatives and rely on diversified funds and bonds, at the price of a large divestment tax bill and daily fines for delay.
Retail trading by thousands of officials and their families would end, but compliance would push them into index funds and managed accounts; minimal effect on the public.

industries.industry: Digital asset platforms and prediction markets
industries.note: The bill extends the ban to digital assets and event contracts, closing a loophole newer trading products would otherwise offer officials; no direct cost to ordinary users.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to four committees with zero cosponsors almost never reach a floor vote; unless Vindman builds cosponsor backing or leadership decides to prioritize a stock-trading ban, this bill will likely sit without action until the Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
